correctness.rationale: For Q=1+x+x^(-1) and p>=5, Q(x) divides Q(x^p) integrally in Laurent polynomials by the action of p on primitive cube roots. Its quotient B has exponents strictly between -p and p, and constant term epsilon_p by extracting x^(p-1) from (1-x)/(1-x^3). Reducing Q^p=Q(x^p) modulo p and cancelling Q in the Laurent domain shows Q^(p-1)=B+pA with integral A of support likewise inside (-p,p). Expanding (Q(x^p)+pQA)^m and cancelling one exact Q, the terms containing at least two p factors remain divisible by p^2. The remaining polynomials give (B+mpA)Q(x^p)^(m-1). Only exponent zero of B and A can pair with an exponent divisible by p, yielding the first formula with p CT(A)=T_(p-1)-epsilon_p. The verified Cao–Sun base-index residue and (1+pu)^m=1+mpu modulo p^2 give the second formula for all positive m, including multiples of p, with no division by a trinomial coefficient. Iteration contributes r signs and total exponent p^r-1. An independent direct binomial summation (`python3 /workspace/reproduce.py`) checked 70 pairs including m=p and 2p, and 9 prime-power instances. The finite checks are not the proof.

evidence: Q has Newton interval [-1,1] and zero as its unique interior lattice point, so the general Laurent constant-term theorem applies. Its modulo-p digit product supplies T_(pm-1)=T_(p-1)T_(m-1) modulo p. The higher-power relation has products involving both the original index and the index after deleting a digit.
broader_coverage.reasoning: The higher-power theorem gives relations among unknown residues; the mod-p result fixes only the zeroth-order factor. The inspected statements do not supply the first-order explicit multiplier at the boundary.

evidence: The published base case determines CT(A) only after the integral quotient B has been constructed and the support separation proved. A coupled recurrence in higher digits does not evaluate the remaining two-digit residues at the prime-square level from that base input alone in the passages examined.
claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: The support-derived lift is the key extra fact needed to turn the known base evaluation into the exact factor for all m. The resulting prime-power evaluation then follows by telescoping the exponents; it does not support an additional originality claim.
searches: Cao–Sun Theorem 1.1(i), Eq. (1.4); Mellit–Vlasenko Theorem 1 and coupled shift; Pan–Sun Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 1.1

evidence: The constant term of Q^n is the coefficient of x^n in (1+x+x^2)^n. Cao–Sun uses the same T_n and epsilon=(p/3); it evaluates T_(p-1) only. Pan–Sun treats T_(pn)-T_n and T_(p^a), not minus-one indices.
equivalent_formulations.reasoning: The audited lift is not a relabeling of an ordinary prime-index congruence, nor is the published m=1 evaluation itself new. Its explicit multiplier is required at all m, even when m or T_(m-1) is zero modulo p.
searches: Central trinomial coefficients modulo prime square, indices pn-1 or p^r-1, digit boundary, constant terms and Dwork congruences

originality.rationale: The inspected literature gives the m=1 base case, a general mod-p digit law, higher-power coupled relations, and stronger results on other indices. The supported distinct claim is the explicit mod-p^2 coefficient on the whole pm-1 family. The prime-power statement is credited as its iteration, not as independent novelty. The bounded comparisons do not establish absolute priority.
residual_risks: An overlooked all-digit or differently normalized supercongruence might subsume the lift. The literature search and inspected indexed results are bounded.
The proofs of older congruences were not all read in full; the comparison is to the identified theorem statements and relevant displayed relations.

value.rationale: This is an exact prime-square lift on a natural full index boundary, well beyond a numerical residue or the published isolated base case. The cyclotomic quotient explains why an entire residue class admits an explicit correction and gives a closed formula for strings of maximal base-p digits without any unit assumption on the smaller trinomial coefficient.
